He appears in an incident that took place in Ephesus: his seven sons, having heard about the power of the name of Jesus and the miracles performed by the apostle Paul, attempted to use that name to cast out demons from a possessed man. Contrary to their expectations, the exorcism spectacularly failed: the demon seized the possessed man and threw him upon them with such violence that they had to flee naked and wounded. This event shows that power over evil spirits is not obtained by merely pronouncing a name, but through true faith in Jesus Christ.
G4630.origine: The name Sceva (Greek Σκευᾶς, Skeuas) is of Hebrew or Aramaic origin. Few ancient sources outside the Bible mention this character. His name appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 19:14.
G4630.emploi: Sceva appears only once in the entire Bible, in Acts 19:14. He is mentioned in passing to identify the father of the seven sons who unsuccessfully attempted to exorcise a demon by invoking the name of Jesus. Paul was in Ephesus at that time and was performing powerful miracles; this context explains why Sceva's sons believed they could imitate these wonders. The incident illustrates the superiority of Jesus' power and the necessity of a genuine relationship with him to act in his name.
G4630.portee: This episode of Sceva's sons teaches Christians that the name of Jesus is not a magic formula that can be invoked without true faith. Spiritual power rests on an authentic relationship with Christ, not on words or rituals. For the believer, it is a warning against spiritual pretension and a call to seek God's power not through techniques, but through trust in Jesus himself.

sens: Equipment and accessories of a ship, everything that serves its operation and navigation
Utensils and equipment that are thrown overboard in case of necessity
G4631.detail:
1. The word refers to the complete equipment of a ship: sails, rigging, anchors, masts, and all objects that allow the boat to navigate and function. It encompasses everything that is part of the material and structure of the vessel, distinct from the cargo. In Acts 27:19, during the terrible storm, the crew deliberately throws these ship's tackle overboard to lighten the ship and increase their chances of survival.
2. The term can also more broadly refer to utensils and equipment that are used or abandoned: in times of danger, one first gets rid of the less essential, which shows the despair and urgency of the situation.
G4631.origine: The Greek word σκευή comes from a root meaning "to prepare, arrange." It is related to σκεῦος (skeuos), which refers to a utensil or manufactured object, and more broadly to anything that is prepared or equipped. The Greek root evokes the idea of something shaped, intentionally arranged to serve a purpose.
G4631.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:19. Paul is traveling by ship to Rome when a violent storm arises in the Mediterranean. The terrified crew, out of resources, throws the ship's tackle overboard to make it lighter and attempt to save themselves. It is a dramatic moment that illustrates the extreme peril: when even the essential equipment of the boat must be sacrificed, it indicates that the situation is desperate.
G4631.portee: This shipwreck narrative reminds the reader that God protects His servant Paul even in the midst of the storm and chaos. The act of throwing the tackle symbolizes the abandonment of all human recourse: only God can save. For the believer, this scene invites recognition that our earthly resources and equipment are insufficient; true security lies in God alone.

sens: an object that contains something: vase, pot, container
an object, thing, material good
the entirety of the belongings of a house or a ship
a person considered as an instrument for a purpose
the human body, physical envelope
G4632.detail:
1. A vessel or container intended to hold something: this is the most common and concrete meaning. In Luke 8:16, a lamp is mentioned that should not be covered with a "vessel" to hide it; in Acts 10:11, a large "sheet" resembling a vessel descends from heaven.
2. An object, a thing, any material good — not just a container. In Matthew 12:29, plundering someone's goods means taking their vessels, their belongings. This conveys the general idea of "possessed thing."
3. The entirety of the belongings and tools of a ship, its rigging and equipment: in Acts 27:17, the vessels of the boat are mentioned, meaning ropes and maneuvering devices.
4. Figuratively, a person themselves, considered as an instrument or container in the service of God. In Acts 9:15, Paul is a "vessel" chosen by God to bear His name. In Romans 9:22-23, some are "vessels of wrath," while others are "vessels of mercy."
5. The human body, the physical envelope where the person resides. In 2 Corinthians 4:7, we carry a treasure in "earthen vessels" — our fragile bodies. In 1 Peter 3:7, the woman is called "the weaker vessel," meaning the more delicate body.
G4632.origine: The Greek word σκεῦος comes from the same root as the verb "to prepare, equip." Its basic image is that of a manufactured object equipped for use. In Hebrew, the corresponding term is כְּלִי (keli), which also means "tool, utensil, instrument, vessel." The notion of "vessel" naturally extends to "object, thing, good," and then, figuratively, to "person" as an instrument or body.
G4632.emploi: The word σκεῦος appears 22 times in the New Testament, primarily in Acts, Paul's epistles, and Revelation. In its concrete sense, it first refers to containers (a lamp covered with a vessel in Luke 8:16), then expands to the goods and belongings of a house (Matthew 12:29, Mark 3:27) or the rigging of a ship (Acts 27:17). It is in Acts 10:11 and 11:5 that the famous vision of a large "sheet" filled with animals, described as a vessel, appears. In a figurative and theological sense, Paul richly develops the image of the vessel to speak of the person: Paul is a "chosen vessel" (Acts 9:15), some are "vessels of wrath" and others "vessels of mercy" (Romans 9:22-23). The expression also applies to the body: in 2 Corinthians 4:7, we are "earthen vessels" carrying a treasure; in 1 Peter 3:7, the woman is the "weaker vessel"; in 1 Thessalonians 4:4, it is about "possessing one's body" as one would possess a vessel.
G4632.portee: This word helps the believer understand their relationship with God. Being a "vessel" means being an instrument shaped to fulfill God's plan — which confers dignity and responsibility. The image of the "earthen vessel" containing a treasure speaks to the fragility of our bodies and the contrast between our weakness and the glory of the Gospel that we carry. Finally, the notion of a vessel invites us to treat the body with respect, not as something contemptible, but as an object chosen by God.

sens: Portable shelter made of fabric stretched over a framework
Mobile structure used for worship and sacrifices
The tabernacle, the portable sanctuary of the people of Israel
Dwelling or habitation, in a figurative sense
Celestial or eternal place of residence
G4633.detail:
1. A tent is primarily a temporary dwelling made of fabric and ropes, which is set up and taken down: Peter proposes to set up three tents for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah on the Mount of Transfiguration (Matthew 17:4), as temporary shelters to stay close to them.
2. A tent can refer to a specialized structure for worship: it is the tabernacle, the portable sanctuary that the Israelites carried in the desert where sacrifices and sacred rituals took place (Hebrews 9:6).
3. The Bible also speaks of the tent of David, a royal dwelling or a symbol of reign (Acts 15:16), and uses "tent" to refer to access to God or worship (Hebrews 13:10).
4. Figuratively, the tent represents a dwelling, a lodging: Abraham, for example, dwelled in a tent during his pilgrimage of faith (Hebrews 11:9).
5. The word can finally refer to eternal dwellings in heaven, the celestial resting places that Jesus promises to those who trust Him (Luke 16:9).
G4633.origine: The Greek word σκηνή comes from a root that evokes the idea of sheltering, covering. In Hebrew, it primarily translates אֹהֶל (ohel, "tent"), but also מִשְׁכָּן (mishkan, "dwelling, sanctuary"): two words that emphasize either the provisional aspect of the dwelling or its sacred role as God's dwelling among men. The biblical context enriches the meaning: a tent is not a permanent building, but a refuge, a mobile and often sacred presence.
G4633.emploi: The word "tent" appears 21 times in the provided usages, mostly in the Epistle to the Hebrews (12 occurrences) and in the Gospels. In the first three Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke), the term refers to the shelters that Peter wants to build during the Transfiguration, a naive image of a desire to prolong a sacred encounter. The Epistle to the Hebrews systematically uses "tent" or "tabernacle" to describe the portable sanctuary of Israel and its ritual organization (Hebrews 9), sometimes in contrast to the celestial and permanent structure of which it was the earthly reflection (Hebrews 8:2, 9:11). Luke 16:9 uses "eternal tabernacles" to speak of heavenly dwellings. Acts cites passages from the Old Testament where the tent of David or the tent of Moloch is mentioned. The meaning thus shifts from the concrete (a mobile dwelling) to the sacred (a place of encounter with God) and to the eternal (a heavenly dwelling).
G4633.portee: Understanding what a tent is helps grasp the spirituality of the Old Testament: God did not dwell in a fixed building, but in the heart of a nomadic camp, sharing the life of His people. This image speaks to us today: our earthly life is a tent, temporary and portable, while God promises us an eternal, stable, and definitive dwelling with Him.

sens: Great Jewish autumn festival celebrated for seven days
Commemoration of the Israelites' dwelling in tents in the desert
Harvest and thanksgiving festival
Pilgrimage moment when Jews went up to Jerusalem
G4634.detail: 1. The Feast of Tabernacles is one of the three major festivals in the Jewish calendar, celebrated in the autumn for seven days. It derives its name from the Greek word σκηνή (skènè), which means "tent" or "temporary dwelling": Jews would build small huts with branches and live in them during the festival to remember the time when their ancestors lived in tents in the desert after the exodus from Egypt (John 7:2). 2. This festival concretely commemorates the passage of the people of Israel through the desert for forty years, under God's protection. By temporarily living in huts, Jews would relive, once a year, the experience of their ancestors who depended entirely on God. 3. It was also a harvest and thanksgiving festival: it celebrated the end of the fruit and wine harvest, an occasion of joy and gratitude to God for His blessings. 4. Jews considered this festival an important religious duty: many would go up to Jerusalem during these seven days to participate in worship at the temple, making it a major moment of popular gathering.
G4634.origine: The Greek word σκηνοπηγία (skènopègia) is composed of σκηνή (skènè, "tent") and the verb πήγνυμι (pègnumi, "to fix", "to set up"), which literally means "the establishment of tents". It is the Greek translation of the Hebrew word סֻכָּה (soukkah), which refers to a hut or temporary shelter. The New Testament adopts the expression used by Hellenized Jews to refer to this ancient festival prescribed by the Law of Moses.
G4634.emploi: The Feast of Tabernacles is mentioned only once in the Gospel of John, in John 7:2, at the beginning of the account where Jesus goes up to this feast. It is on this occasion that Jesus teaches in the temple and the Jews seek Him out (John 7:11-13). The feast was prescribed in the Old Testament Law as one of the three major festivals to which all Jewish males were required to go to Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 16:16). It held great religious and cultural significance: it was a time of joy, communal celebration, and renewal of the historical memory of the people of Israel.
G4634.portee: For the Christian reader, this feast reminds us that God walked with His people in the desert and protected them. Understanding this feast while reading the Gospel helps to grasp the context in which Jesus teaches and acts: it is at the heart of the celebration of God's faithfulness to His people that Jesus reveals Himself as the one who gives living water and light (John 7:37-39, 8:12). It also shows how Jesus fits into Jewish religious traditions to fulfill what they foreshadowed.

sens: One who makes and sews tents
One who practices this trade as a livelihood
G4635.detail: 1. A tentmaker is someone who makes tents — they cut, assemble, and sew fabric (usually canvas or goat hair) to create portable shelters. This was a widely practiced profession in the ancient Mediterranean world, serving both nomadic families and travelers, merchants, and soldiers. 2. As a profession, it was an honest and respectable trade, neither wealthy nor impoverished. Paul himself practiced it: in Corinth, he worked with Aquila and Priscilla, who shared the same trade (Acts 18:3). This allowed him to support himself while preaching the Gospel.
G4635.origine: The Greek word σκηνοποιός (skēnopoios) is formed from two elements: σκηνή (skēnē), "tent, tabernacle", and ποιέω (poieō), "to make, to create". The literal meaning is therefore "one who makes tents". It is a transparent compound that simply describes the profession by its two components: to make (ποιέω) a tent (σκηνή).
G4635.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:3, during Paul's second visit to Corinth. The account specifies that Paul "had the same trade" as Aquila and Priscilla, which explains why he stayed with them and worked with them. This mention reveals not only Paul's profession but also his conviction not to live as a parasite off his communities: he earned his bread by the work of his hands, a principle he would later remind them of in his letters. The trade of tentmaking was common enough that other artisans in the same field could be found in the Jewish diaspora.
G4635.portee: This word reminds us of an often-overlooked aspect of the apostle Paul: he was not a professional preacher living off his listeners, but a worker who toiled hard with his hands. His example invites the Christian reader to honor manual labor and to see it as a form of dignity, not a secondary status compared to spiritual ministry. Paul thus unites apostolic action and daily work, showing that one can serve God without detaching from the concrete realities of economic life.

sens: Mobile shelter made of fabric or skins stretched over a framework
Figuratively, the human body considered as a temporary dwelling for the soul
G4636.detail:
1. A tent is a portable shelter made of fabric or skins stretched over a framework: it is the dwelling of nomads and travelers, easy to set up and take down. It is the same word as "tabernacle", the sacred tent of Israelite worship.
2. The apostle Paul uses the image of the tent to speak of the body: just as a tent is temporary and can be folded up, the earthly body is a temporary dwelling for the soul, destined to be left behind one day. In 2 Corinthians 5:1, he writes, "if this tent we live in on earth is destroyed" to express that death dissolves our fleshly envelope. This image shows that our stay on earth is not permanent, but that we await "an eternal dwelling not made by human hands."
G4636.origine: The Greek word σκῆνος (skēnos) is close to σκηνή (skēnē), which also means "tent" or "tabernacle". It comes from the idea of constructing a temporary shelter. In the Greek Old Testament, this vocabulary translates the Hebrew אֹהֶל (ohel), which refers to the tent, including Israel's portable sanctuary.
G4636.emploi: The word appears only twice in 2 Corinthians 5:1 and 5:4. Paul uses it metaphorically to describe the body as a temporary residence: in 5:1, he mentions its destruction (death), and in 5:4, he speaks of the groaning of one who resides in this tent, longing to put on incorruptibility eternal. It is a coherent image of the human condition in the flesh and the Christian hope of shedding mortality.
G4636.portee: This biblical image of the body as a "tent" corrects a fusionist view of body and soul: it reminds us that our body is not our permanent identity, but a dwelling we will leave. It strengthens faith in the resurrection and eternal life, and invites the believer not to cling idolatrously to earthly realities, while honoring this body as the temple of the Holy Spirit during our life on earth.

sens: Establish one's dwelling, residence in a place
Temporarily reside under a tent or in a shelter
Dwell, remain in the company of someone
Take place and establish one's permanent presence
G4637.detail:
1. The most basic meaning is to establish one's home, to live in a place. It conveys the idea of settling permanently: God "will dwell with them" (Revelation 21:3), meaning He will establish His permanent presence among men.
2. The word also evokes the image of a tent or temporary dwelling: when it is said that God "will pitch His tent among them" (Revelation 7:15), it refers to the tent of the tabernacle in the desert, that mobile sanctuary which was God's house among the people of Israel.
3. To dwell also means to reside somewhere, to be present: "those who dwell in heaven" (Revelation 12:12 and 13:6) refers to the inhabitants of heaven, those whose home is in heaven.
4. In John 1:14, "the Word dwelt among us," the verb suggests that God the Son established His residence in human flesh, pitched His tent among humanity: this is the incarnation, God taking up physical residence among men.
G4637.origine: The word comes from the Greek σκηνή (skènè), which means "tent" or "tabernacle." This root evokes the primitive idea of pitching a tent, taking shelter under a temporary roof. In Hebrew, the verb שָׁכַן (shakan), from which to dwell is derived, has the same meaning: to reside, to dwell, particularly when speaking of God who places His presence in the tabernacle or temple. The Greek word has taken on a strong theological significance: it describes not only a physical dwelling but the presence of God among His people.
G4637.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Gospels and Revelation. In John 1:14, it expresses the incarnation of the divine Word in Jesus Christ, with the idea of a transformative presence: the Word becomes flesh and establishes His dwelling among humans. In Revelation, it appears several times to describe the divine and heavenly presence: God pitches His tent over the redeemed (7:15), the saints dwell in heaven (12:12, 13:6), and at the end of time, God will dwell definitively with men (21:3). Each time, the word carries the theological weight of God's established and stable presence, whether as an incarnate reality or as a heavenly and eternal destiny.
G4637.portee: This word reminds the reader that God is not distant or abstract: He chooses to establish His dwelling among humans, first in Jesus Christ made flesh, then in remaining with His people for eternity. It is a promise of divine proximity, of intimate communion between God and man — the opposite of abandonment or absence. The verb invites the Christian to understand that the incarnation is not an isolated event, but the beginning of a permanent divine presence that culminates in the new creation.

sens: A tent or temporary shelter
The tabernacle or temple, the place where God dwells
The human body, considered as a temporary dwelling for the soul
G4638.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a tent, that portable shelter made of canvas or skin that nomads and pilgrims used for lodging. It is a provisional dwelling, meant to be left behind.
2. By sacred extension, it refers to the tabernacle or the temple in Jerusalem, the "dwelling" of God among His people. In Acts 7:46, Stephen speaks of the dwelling that David wished to build for God, referring to the temple.
3. Poetically and spiritually, Paul and Peter use this word to refer to the human body. Like a tent, the body is a temporary shelter: in 2 Peter 1:13-14, Peter speaks of this "tent" that he must soon leave — he knows that death is approaching and that his soul will leave its fleshly envelope.
G4638.origine: The word comes from the verb "skēnoō" which means "to pitch a tent" or "to dwell under a tent." It thus designates the place where one camps. In Hebrew, it primarily translates the word "ohel" (tent) in the Greek Old Testament. The family of words also includes "skēnē" (tent, dwelling) and "skēnos" (tent). The basic image is that of a provisional lodging, established and folded according to needs.
G4638.emploi: The word appears only 3 times in the New Testament. In Acts 7:46, it designates the temple as the dwelling of God. But it is especially in 2 Peter 1:13-14 that it takes on a strong spiritual meaning: Peter uses the term "tent" to speak of the body, emphasizing its ephemeral nature in the face of eternity. This biblical image, classic in Hebrew thought, aims to remind that the body is merely a temporary shelter that the soul must leave at death.
G4638.portee: This image of the "tent" or "temporary dwelling" speaks to the heart of the Christian: it reminds him of the reality of the present world. The body is not our final destination; we are on pilgrimage in this world. This perspective helps to transcend attachment to visible and transient things, and to fix hope on what is eternal and unshakeable.

sens: A dark area created by an object that intercepts light
Refuge or protection provided by shade
An image or vague outline of a reality
What is temporary or illusory compared to reality
Ignorance and error (shadow of death)
G4639.detail:
1. In the literal sense, shadow is the dark area created when something intercepts light. In Mark 4:32, the mustard seed becomes a great tree under which the birds can shelter: it is the cool and protective shade of a tree in the sun.

2. The shadow offers refuge and protection: that is why it is sought after. In Acts 5:15, Peter's mere shadow is enough for the sick to hope for healing — the shadow becomes a sign of the saving presence.

3. The shadow is also an image, a vague outline of a more true reality. In Hebrews 8:5, the temple worship is only the shadow and image of heavenly things — a sketch on earth of the reality of heaven.

4. Compared to the body or the reality itself (Colossians 2:17, Hebrews 10:1), the shadow is what passes and disappears. The Law and its rites were only the shadow of things to come; the body, the full reality, is Christ.

5. The expression "shadow of death" (Matthew 4:16, Luke 1:79) refers to spiritual ignorance, the darkness of sin: a deadly shadow from which only the light of Christ can rescue us.
G4639.origine: The Greek word σκιά comes from a root denoting the darkness caused by the interception of light. In Hebrew, it primarily translates צֵל (ṣēl), the shadow of a tree or rock, a natural refuge. The expression "shadow of death" translates the Hebrew צַלְמָוֶת (ṣalmāvet), which plays on the assonance between צֵל (shadow) and מָוֶת (death): a shadow that is also deadly. The Bible transposes the word from the concrete (the shadow of a tree) to the figurative (the shadow of divine realities, of the old Law).
G4639.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament translated as "shadow." It is first used in the physical sense: the shadow of a tree where birds shelter (Mark 4:32), or that of Peter healing the sick (Acts 5:15). But most uses are figurative: the shadow of death denotes spiritual ignorance and sin from which the light of Christ frees us (Matthew 4:16, Luke 1:79). Finally, in the epistles, the shadow takes on a typological meaning: the temple worship, the Law, the prescriptions are the shadow of heavenly realities and of Christ; the shadow gives way to the body, the prefiguration to the reality (Colossians 2:17, Hebrews 8:5 and 10:1). The word thus moves from the sensible to the spiritual and from the temporary to the eternal.
G4639.portee: This word teaches us that everything we experience in the Old Testament — worship, the Law, promises — was only a shadow of the reality revealed in Christ. It invites us not to stop at appearances or vague outlines, but to seek the substance, the fullness that God offers us. It also shows that spiritual ignorance and sin are a shadow, a darkness: only the light of Christ dispels it. Finally, it reminds us that God already grants us a protective shadow, a refuge in Him, even now.

sens: To make a jump, a quick and involuntary movement of the body or a part of the body
To manifest through a sudden jerk: to tremble, to palpitate (referring to the heart or the child in the womb)
To express a strong emotion — joy, elation — through this movement of the body
G4640.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes a physical jump or leap: a sudden and lively movement of the body. In Luke 1:41, the child John the Baptist "leaped" in Elizabeth's womb — a real, perceptible bodily gesture to the mother.

2. This involuntary movement can express an instinctive reaction of the heart or body in response to something: a jolt of emotion. In Luke 1:44, Mary says that the child "leaped for joy," which shows that the leaping of the body translates a deep inner joy.

3. The word is also used to urge someone to manifest their joy through movement and exultation. In Luke 6:23, the disciples are invited to "leap for joy" to express their elation at the promised reward — it is a call to react with their whole being.
G4640.origine: The Greek verb σκιρτάω comes from a root that fundamentally means "to leap, to jump." The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament, uses it to render the Hebrew רָקַד ("to dance, to leap") in the Psalms, notably to describe the mountains that "leap" in Psalms 114:4-6. The word emphasizes the lively and visible movement of the body.
G4640.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, all occurrences being in Luke. In Luke 1:41 and 1:44, in the account of Mary's Visit to Elizabeth, it describes the movement of the fetus John the Baptist, perceived by his mother as a reaction to the presence of Jesus in Mary — a very sensitive and concrete detail that showed Elizabeth that something extraordinary was happening. In Luke 6:23, Jesus uses the verb to exhort his disciples to an overflowing joy that is visibly expressed, despite persecutions: it is an invitation to total joy of body and soul combined.
G4640.portee: This word reminds us that biblical faith is not merely an intellectual or spiritual matter: it is embodied in the whole body. The emotion of joy — that of Elizabeth discovering the mystery of the Incarnation, that of the persecuted disciple who rejoices nonetheless — is visibly and physically manifested. It is also a call to an overflowing joy that springs involuntarily from the heart and is expressed by all that we are.

sens: Obstinate refusal to listen or submit
Closing of the mind and conscience to the truth
Spiritual insensitivity to God's calls
G4641.detail:
1. Hardness of heart describes a voluntary and tenacious resistance to God's will or to His messengers. It is not mere distraction, but a deliberate refusal to obey. When Jesus explains to His disciples that Moses allowed divorce "because of the hardness of your hearts" (Matthew 19:8 and Mark 10:5), he shows that this closing of the heart drives people away from God's plan and leads them to seek legal loopholes to satisfy their desires.
2. It is also a form of spiritual blindness: the soul becomes insensitive to the calls, signs, and proofs that God places on its path. The eleven apostles themselves manifest this hardness when they refuse to believe in the resurrection despite the testimonies of the women and other disciples: Jesus "rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart" (Mark 16:14), showing that their unbelief arises from a closing of the heart, not from mere ignorance.
G4641.origine: The Greek word σκληροκαρδία is composed of σκληρός (sklēros, "hard, rigid, like a stone") and καρδία (kardia, "heart"). This image of the heart becoming hard as stone evokes the Hebrew Old Testament: the expression "uncircumcised heart" (לֵבָב עׇרְלָה) is found in Deuteronomy 10:16 and Jeremiah 4:4, where the uncircumcision of the heart symbolizes a voluntary refusal to submit to God, just as physical uncircumcision marked exclusion from the covenant. The hardness of heart opposes a receptive, flexible heart capable of repentance and change.
G4641.emploi: This word appears only three times in the New Testament (Matthew 19:8, Mark 10:5, Mark 16:14), always in the mouth of Jesus or to describe the disciples. In Matthew 19:8 and Mark 10:5, Jesus explains that the Mosaic permission for divorce was a concession because of human hardness: God tolerates evil without approving it, in order to reduce suffering in a sinful world. In Mark 16:14, Jesus rebukes the apostles for their hardness of heart combined with unbelief: it even prevents the direct witnesses of miracles from recognizing the resurrection. The word always denotes a dangerous state of soul, a closing to God's action.
G4641.portee: This word highlights that sin is not merely an external weakness, but an internal closing, a stiffness of heart that resists God. It calls the believer to examine themselves: to identify the moments when their own heart hardens, when they consciously resist what God shows them. The solution is not legal or external, but spiritual: it is to ask God for a new heart, flexible, receptive to His voice.

sens: Hard to the touch, rough to the sensation
Difficult to bear, painful to the ear or heart
Violent, impetuous (referring to natural forces)
Severe, inflexible, merciless (referring to a person)
Not easily welcomed or accepted
G4642.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: something hard to the touch, rough, that resists. It is the opposite of soft or tender.

2. Figuratively, a hard word is difficult to hear, painful to receive. In John 6:60, the disciples say that Jesus' word about the bread of life is "hard" — it shocks, it exceeds what they expected to hear.

3. A force is hard when it is violent and impetuous. In James 3:4, hard winds shake ships with brute force.

4. A hard person is severe, inflexible, without compassion. The servant in Matthew 25:24 describes his master as hard: someone who demands much and spares nothing.

5. To kick against the goads (Acts 9:5 and 26:14): it is hard, meaning futile and harmful, to resist God's will. It is an image of an animal that rears against the goad and injures itself.
G4642.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to dry": what is dry becomes hard. In Hebrew, the word קָשָׁה (qasha) has the same meaning and describes what is stiff, inflexible, difficult. The word appears mainly in the Greek of the New Testament to translate this Hebrew. The family includes compounds that retain this idea of hardness or resistance.
G4642.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament. It is first used for the hardness of a person: Jesus describes a strict master (Matthew 25:24), and Paul speaks of a heart hardened by resistance to God (Acts 9:5, 26:14). It qualifies a word difficult to accept (John 6:60). It also describes violent natural phenomena: impetuous winds shaking a ship (James 3:4), or injurious words that strike hard (Jude 1:15). The context always shows a certain resistance or a negative charge.
G4642.portee: This word helps the reader understand that God's will cannot be resisted without consequence: wanting to stand against it is a hardness against oneself. It also shows that the Gospel may seem difficult or shocking to the ear, but that this apparent hardness hides a wisdom that only faith can accept. It is a call to soften, to allow oneself to be transformed rather than to harden.

sens: State of the heart closed to the voice of God
Obstinate refusal to repent
Moral and spiritual hardness
G4643.detail:
1. Hardening primarily refers to the physical hardness of a material — like a stone that does not yield, that refuses to be shaped. The Bible transposes this image to the human heart: a hardened heart is a heart that has become impermeable, no longer allowing itself to be touched by grace or the voice of God.

2. It is particularly the refusal to repent, the absence of regret in the face of sin. In Romans 2:5, Paul depicts someone who is storing up wrath precisely because of their hardening — they refuse to change despite warnings and evidence of God's justice. Their heart remains closed while everything around them cries out: "Return!"

3. It is a form of voluntary rebellion, not an involuntary weakness. Hardening implies that one has had the opportunity to yield, that one has heard the call, but has chosen to remain unmoved, insensitive, and unyielding in evil.
G4643.origine: The word comes from the Greek σκληρός (sklēros), which means "hard" in the physical sense. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often translates קְשִׁי (queshî), which also means "hardness" or "stubbornness." This image of a hard heart is deeply biblical: from Exodus onward, Pharaoh's heart was hardened in the face of the plagues. The noun σκληρότης forms a family with the adjective sklēros (hard) and the verb σκληρύνω (to harden), frequently used to speak of the obstinate refusal to believe.
G4643.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 2:5. Paul uses it to describe the heart of one who rejects the message of repentance and stores up divine wrath. It is a continuation of Paul's reasoning on God's judgment: the cardinal virtue of the impenitent is not strength, but the sterile illusion of remaining unyielding in sin. The context shows that this hardening is not a condemnation of fate, but personal responsibility — one hardens oneself by refusing grace.
G4643.portee: For the believer, this word is a warning: it reminds that the heart can gradually close, that it is possible to resist the Spirit for so long that one ends up no longer hearing Him. It is a call to remain vigilant, to keep the heart tender to the voice of God. Conversely, it assures that no one is condemned by fate to hardening — everyone remains free to return.

sens: Having a neck that is tense, stiff, inflexible
Figuratively, rebellious and insubordinate, refusing to obey or submit
G4644.detail:
1. In the literal sense, "stiff neck" refers to someone whose neck is tense and rigid, incapable of bending or turning. The image is that of a stubborn beast of burden or a person who stiffens their neck to resist.
2. Figuratively, the word describes an attitude of rebellion and obstinate refusal. In Acts 7:51, Stephen accuses the Jews of being "stiff-necked": they refuse to submit to the Holy Spirit, just as their ancestors refused to obey God. It is the image of voluntary resistance, a stubborn insubordination towards God.
G4644.origine: The word is composed of "sklēros" (hard, stiff, tough) and "trachēlos" (neck). The image comes from pastoral and agricultural life: a beast with a stiff neck refuses to be directed by the shepherd or the plowman. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the expression "stiff neck" (עֹרֶף קָשֶׁה) for the same idea: a people that does not want to bend before God.
G4644.emploi: This word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 7:51, in Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin. Stephen uses it to accuse the Jewish authorities of systematically resisting the Holy Spirit, just as their ancestors had done. The adjective recalls a classic biblical language: the Old Testament already described Israel with this image when it rebelled against the Law and the prophets. Stephen reminds of this continuity of rebellion, to show that resistance to Christ and the Spirit is merely the culmination of a long history of disobedience.
G4644.portee: This image invites self-examination: am I like an animal with a stiff neck, or am I ready to bend under God's hand? It reminds that rebellion is never hidden — it is as visible as a beast stiffening its neck. It calls for humility and obedience to the Holy Spirit, especially when God speaks through His Word.

sens: to make hard, rigid, impermeable (in the physical sense)
to become insensitive, impermeable to truth or to God
to refuse to listen, to repent, to change
to allow one's heart to be hardened by sin or unbelief
G4645.detail:
1. In the literal sense, to harden means to make something hard and resistant, as one hardens a material. The Bible uses this word mainly in a figurative sense, for the soul and the heart.

2. To harden the heart is to make it impermeable to God, to the calls of His grace. It is to become insensitive to His voice, like dead wood that can no longer bend. Pharaoh is the major biblical example: his heart hardened in the face of God's signs.

3. To harden also means to refuse to listen and to repent. In Romans 9:18, God "hardens whom He wills": He abandons the one who obstinately resists the truth, leaving them imprisoned by their unbelief.

4. The heart hardens progressively through the seduction of sin (Hebrews 3:13). Each refusal to hear God's voice deepens the chasm, each act of disobedience makes the soul more deaf and harder.
G4645.origine: The Greek word σκληρύνω comes from the adjective σκληρός ("hard, rigid, rough"). It often translates in Greek from the Old Testament the Hebrew קָשָׁה (kashâh, to harden) and חָזַק (chazaq, to strengthen, to become strong). The image is that of a material becoming hard and unyielding: a hardened heart no longer allows itself to be impressed, it opposes fierce resistance.
G4645.emploi: The New Testament uses this word 6 times, mainly in the Epistle to the Hebrews and in Paul's writings. It almost always refers to the hardening of the heart in the face of God and grace. In Romans 9:18, it is God who hardens, in a mystery of justice: He abandons the one who persists in rebellion. In Hebrews 3, the word recurs as a repeated warning (verses 8, 13, 15, 4:7): the readers must not reproduce Israel's hardening in the desert, which refused to enter God's rest. In Acts 19:9, Paul's opponents harden themselves in unbelief and public contradiction.
G4645.portee: This word challenges us regarding our own responsiveness to God's call. The hardening of the heart does not happen all at once: it begins with a slight resistance, then worsens through the habit of sin and refusal to listen. God's grace continually calls, but the one who closes their ear risks that their heart will close as well. It is a warning: today, again, is the day to allow oneself to be softened by the voice of God.

sens: Not straight, bending or curling
Presenting difficulties, obstacles
Deviating from the right path, from honesty
Contrary to justice and righteousness
G4646.detail:
1. In a literal sense, twisted describes physically what is not straight: a winding road, a bumpy path that curls upon itself. In Luke 3:5, the prophet Isaiah announces that "the twisted will be made straight" — the image is that of the steep and winding paths of Judea that must be flattened.
2. By extension, twisted can qualify what is difficult, harsh, or complicated to endure. In 1 Peter 2:18, the "harsh" masters are literally "of a twisted character" — like a bumpy road, they are not easy to follow.
3. In a moral sense, twisted designates one who deviates from righteousness, from integrity, one who does not walk in justice. It is the opposite of one who "walks straight."
4. For the Apostle Paul in Philippians 2:15, being "perverse" means being morally twisted — unlike the children of God who are "blameless," it represents a generation that strays from God and His justice. In Acts 2:40, Peter calls to flee from "this perverse generation," one that resists the Word and refuses salvation.
G4646.origine: The Greek word skolios comes from a root that describes what is bent or curved. The basic image is physical: that of a road that does not go straight, that winds, that zigzags. The corresponding Hebrew word in the Greek Old Testament is often עִקֵּשׁ (iqquèsh) or עָקַשׁ (aqash), which carry the same idea of curvature. In Greek, skolios directly opposes orthós (straight) and euthús (straight-line): where one means the straight line, the other means deviation.
G4646.emploi: The word appears only 4 times in the New Testament, but in very important contexts. In Luke 3:5, it takes up Isaiah's prophecy about preparing the way of the Lord: the material obstacles (ravines, mountains) and the curves of the road symbolize everything that hinders the coming of Christ. In the other three occurrences (Acts 2:40, Philippians 2:15, 1 Peter 2:18), the word has lost its literal meaning to become entirely moral and spiritual. Peter and Paul designate by "perverse" or "harsh" a generation or group that strays from God and refuses the Gospel — what is perverse is one who "refuses to be made straight," who refuses the message of salvation or divine justice.
G4646.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that God wants to straighten what is twisted in us — our detours, our deviations from the truth, our compromises with sin. He invites us to flee from a "perverse" generation to walk in righteousness. It is also an encouragement: even when everything around seems twisted and corrupt (in the world or in our relationships), God calls us to shine like blameless children.

sens: Painful prick embedded in the flesh
Obstacle or affliction sent to humiliate and test
Means of grace that reminds us of our weakness
G4647.detail:
1. A thorn is literally a small point, a spine, or a fragment that embeds itself in the skin and causes pain: it is the concrete image of the word. Paul uses this image in 2 Corinthians 12:7 to describe a physical or spiritual affliction that continually torments him.
2. In biblical language, the thorn represents an affliction sent by God to humble one who might become proud: it is a constant goad, like a thorn that continually reminds of its presence. For Paul, it serves to keep him humble despite the extraordinary visions he has received.
3. Thus, the thorn becomes an instrument of paradoxical grace: although painful, it protects the soul from pride by forcing it to rely on God's power rather than on its own strength.
G4647.origine: The Greek word skolops literally means "that which is pointed," from a root that evokes sharpness. It primarily designates a sharp stake or a pointed pole. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates several Hebrew words designating thorns or prickly obstacles (like שֵׂךְ in Numbers 33:55, סִיר in Hosea 2:6). The word has evolved from the concrete meaning of "stake" to the figurative meaning of "moral or physical prick."
G4647.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: 2 Corinthians 12:7. Paul speaks of a "thorn in the flesh" that he asked God three times to remove, but which was left as a means of grace. This affliction — which has been variously identified as an illness, an infirmity, or persistent opposition — symbolizes the tension between the greatness of Paul's spiritual experiences and his human fragility. The image of the thorn, borrowed from the Old Testament where God warns that enemies will be thorns for Israel, takes on a positive meaning for Paul: what hurts becomes what saves from pride.
G4647.portee: This image speaks to the heart of the Christian confronted with suffering or a persistent trial: it invites him to see in it not an arbitrary punishment, but an instrument of God's tenderness that wants to keep him close and preserve him from the illusion of his own strength. It comforts by showing that even the greatest apostle remains limited and dependent, and that God accepts this weakness to manifest His power.

sens: Look attentively, observe
Direct attention towards something or someone
Be careful not to fall into a trap or error
Consider, reflect on
G4648.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to look attentively, to observe something or someone. It is to set one's gaze on something to see it clearly. In 2 Corinthians 4:18, Paul says "we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen": it is about intentionally directing one's attention to what truly matters.

2. The verb also means to direct attention towards a person or situation. In Philippians 3:17, the apostle says "keep your eyes on those who walk according to the pattern you have in us": it is about fixing one's gaze on these people to imitate them.

3. Very often, take heed means to be careful of a danger, to watch out for a trap. In Romans 16:17, Paul exhorts to "take heed to those who cause divisions": it is a cautious vigilance in the face of a threat. In Galatians 6:1, "take heed to yourself, lest you also be tempted": it is to watch over one's own weakness.

4. The verb can finally mean to consider, to reflect on something. In Philippians 2:4, "consider also the interests of others": it is to give attention to something in one's reflection.
G4648.origine: The word comes from σκοπός (scopos), which designates the goal one looks at, the target or point of aim. To take heed therefore first implies the image of the gaze turned towards something specific, like someone aiming at a target. The root would evoke the action of looking towards a focal point. That is why the verb means both "to look" and "to pay attention to," as if one keeps their eyes fixed on something so as not to lose sight of it.
G4648.emploi: The verb σκοπέω appears 6 times in the New Testament, primarily in Paul. It is translated as "take heed" (3 times), "look" (1 time), "consider" (1 time), and "gaze" (1 time). In the three passages from Luke, Romans, and Galatians, it expresses pastoral vigilance: being careful of a spiritual danger or one's own vulnerability. In 2 Corinthians 4:18 and Philippians 3:17, it means rather to fix one's gaze or attention on something positive: what is invisible and eternal, or a model to imitate. In Philippians 2:4, it is to consider the interests of others with attention. The meaning thus varies from cautious vigilance to benevolent attention.
G4648.portee: This verb invites us to examine where our gaze and attention are directed, which shapes our lives. Watching over oneself and our brothers is to exercise loving spiritual vigilance. But also, learning to look towards what is invisible and eternal rather than towards appearances, and to consider the needs of others as our own: this is how this biblical verb shapes the heart of the disciple.

sens: the target or point towards which one directs their gaze
the final objective towards which one strives
the prize or reward that one aims for
that which gives direction and meaning to life
G4649.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes a target or mark that one fixes their gaze upon — like a point of aim that guides the archer or the runner. Paul uses it in Philippians 3:14: he runs "toward the goal," meaning towards a specific objective that concentrates all his efforts.

2. By extension, it is the objective or destination that one intends to reach, the intention that guides our actions. For Paul, this goal is not a vain earthly ambition: it is God's heavenly calling in Christ Jesus, the reward that awaits him.

3. The goal also refers to the prize or reward that one hopes to win at the end of their race. Paul combines both images: he runs towards a specific destination to grasp the prize of the heavenly calling — just like the ancient runner who fixes his eyes on the prize of gold before accelerating.

4. Spiritually, the word speaks of that which gives direction and meaning to the entire life of the believer. To have a goal in this sense is to live with a clear and holy intention: to orient each day, each choice, each effort towards God and His promise.
G4649.origine: The word comes from the Greek "skopéō," which means "to look, to examine." The starting image is that of a gaze fixed on an object: that is why "skopos" primarily designates a watcher or observer (one who looks attentively to monitor), and then the target itself that one looks at. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb "tzafah," which means "to watch, to scrutinize." The word has retained this idea of concentrating one's gaze: one who looks intensely at a specific point to not lose sight of it.
G4649.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 3:14, where Paul uses it to express the central objective of his life as a believer and apostle. This unique usage makes the word all the more significant: Paul chooses this term to speak of the supreme goal of the Christian, the heavenly calling promised by God. The context shows that the goal is not a mere earthly aspiration, but the eternal crown attached to faithfulness in Christ. This uniqueness in the New Testament also suggests that Paul borrows a sporting and concrete language (the runner, the track, the prize) to make clear and vivid the idea of a life entirely oriented towards God.
G4649.portee: This word invites the Christian to examine their own life: do we have a clear and holy goal, or are we living adrift, scattered among a thousand small concerns? Like Paul who runs towards the prize of the heavenly calling, we are called to fix our gaze on the supreme objective: union with Christ and eternal life with God. It is a word of clarity and encouragement: naming the goal is already to orient each step. For one who lives without a goal, it is a call to stand up and find their direction in God's promise.

sens: Scatter, put to flight (sheep, a crowd)
Separate, divide (a group, disciples)
Distribute, give generously (goods, help)
G4650.detail:
1. To disperse primarily means to physically scatter: the wolf disperses the sheep of the flock by putting them to flight (John 10:12), each fleeing in a different direction. It is the image of order destroyed.
2. The word takes on a spiritual meaning: one who does not gather with Jesus disperses — he divides, separates the disciples instead of uniting them (Matthew 12:30; Luke 11:23). It is an act of opposition, a force that disintegrates.
3. Finally, to disperse can mean to distribute, to spread generously: "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor" (2 Corinthians 9:9). The word here takes on a nuance of blessing: to disperse goods is to give them widely to those in need.
G4650.origine: The verb comes from a root expressing the idea of scattering, fragmenting. In common Greek and among poets, it replaces the old word σκεδάννυμι. In Hebrew, it often corresponds to פּוּץ (pouts, "to disperse"), particularly in the Psalms and the prophets where this verb describes the rout of an army or the deployment of a people.
G4650.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the New Testament, primarily in John. In Matthew and Luke, it opposes "gather" (συνάγειν): one who does not gather with Jesus (the master of the flock) disperses — it is a word of clear division. John uses it twice: for the sheep that the wolf disperses (John 10:12), an image of the flock's vulnerability without a good shepherd, and for the disciples scattered after Jesus' arrest (John 16:32), where each goes their own way. Paul, in quoting Psalm 112, uses "disperse" to describe the generosity of the righteous who gives to the poor (2 Corinthians 9:9): the same word shifts from the sense of separation to that of beneficial diffusion.
G4650.portee: This word reveals the force of division or unity at play in Jesus' ministry. Each must choose: to gather with him or, by their absence, contribute to dispersing. For the believer, it is a call to remain connected to the body of Christ and not to be fragmented. Moreover, the link with generosity (2 Corinthians 9:9) shows that "to disperse" is not always bad: giving one's goods is also to disperse them, but for life and blessing.

sens: Venomous terrestrial animal with pincers and a tail equipped with a stinger
Creature capable of stinging and causing pain
Symbol of what is dangerous and hostile
G4651.detail: 1. The scorpion is a real animal that people in the Middle East were well acquainted with: a crawling beast with front pincers and a curved tail armed with a venomous stinger. Jesus speaks of it as a dangerous terrestrial creature, alongside snakes (Luke 10:19). It is an animal one can walk on. 2. What defines the scorpion is its ability to sting and cause suffering. Jesus says: if he asks for an egg, his father will not give him a scorpion instead (Luke 11:12), for the scorpion is good for nothing, it only brings pain. In the visions of Revelation, the creatures have "tails like scorpions" with stingers, and it is precisely "the power to harm men for five months" (Revelation 9:10). 3. In figurative language, the scorpion becomes the symbol of the enemy — a hostile, invisible, or unexpected force that injures when one least expects it. In the apocalyptic vision, it represents armed malice that torments without killing.
G4651.origine: The Greek word σκορπίος comes from a root meaning "to sting" or "to tear." In Hebrew, the animal is called עַקְרָב (aqrav), etymologically linked to the idea of kicking or striking. The word describes the animal by its characteristic action: it stings. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this Greek word regularly replaces the Hebrew word. The family of the word includes other Greek terms evoking piercing or damage.
G4651.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, all in the Gospels of Luke and Revelation. In Luke, Jesus uses the scorpion concretely: he speaks of the snakes and scorpions that his disciples will tread on without harm (Luke 10:19), and he cites the scorpion as the anti-gift that no father would ever substitute for an egg requested by his son (Luke 11:12). In Revelation, the context becomes entirely visionary: the creatures of the fifth trumpet have the power of scorpions (Revelation 9:3, 5, 10). The scorpion there embodies a power of torment and plague, which injures without killing, which causes suffering for a determined period (five months). The real animal becomes an image of spiritual adversity.
G4651.portee: For the Christian reader, the scorpion reminds us that there are real, concrete, or spiritual dangers that seek to harm us. Jesus assures his disciples that they will have the power to neutralize them (Luke 10:19), which encourages trust even in the face of threats. Understanding that God will never give us evil where we expect good (Luke 11:12) strengthens our confidence in His goodness. In Revelation, the scorpion shows that even divine punishments are not total destruction, but can be calls to repentance: they torment, but leave time to return to God.

sens: Complete darkness, absence of light
Spiritual state of blindness or moral obscurity
Corruption of judgment or malice of heart
G4652.detail:
1. The word primarily describes physical darkness, the absence of light — the direct opposite of what is bright and clear. This is the starting image: the darkness in which nothing can be seen.
2. Jesus uses it figuratively to speak of the eye "in bad condition" (Matthew 6:23, Luke 11:34): it then refers to spiritual blindness, the inability to perceive truth and goodness. When the intention of the heart is evil, it is as if the inside is plunged into darkness.
3. By extension, the word evokes moral blindness or corruption of judgment: one who does not see clearly morally lives as if in darkness, unable to discern good from evil. In Luke 11:36, Jesus promises that the whole body will be "full of light" if no part is "in darkness" — the idea is that the righteousness of the heart fills the whole being with clarity.
G4652.origine: The word comes from the root σκότος (darkness) which primarily denotes the physical absence of light. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it corresponds mainly to the word חֹשֶׁךְ (hoshekh), primordial darkness or the void of light. The Bible regularly uses the imagery of darkness and light to oppose evil to good, ignorance to knowledge, death to life — a powerful and universal image.
G4652.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all cases in Luke and Matthew in the same teaching of Jesus about the eye as the "lamp of the body." Jesus contrasts the eye "in good condition" (which makes the body full of light) with the eye "in bad condition" (which plunges the body into darkness). The image of the eye symbolizes the intention of the heart, the righteousness of judgment: a righteous heart allows divine light to illuminate the whole life; an evil or blinded heart confines the whole being in darkness. This is a teaching on spiritual coherence — one cannot serve God and money, for this divides the heart and creates a false light that is in reality darkness.
G4652.portee: This word invites the reader to examine their own heart: is their spiritual vision clear or obscured? Are they seeking the light of God or confining themselves in compromises that tarnish their judgment? Jesus teaches that inner clarity comes from a right intention directed solely toward God. It is an invitation to sincerity and alignment of the heart with the truth.

sens: Absence of physical light, obscurity
That which is hidden, secret
Spiritual state of ignorance of God and good
Opposition to the reign of God and His light
G4653.detail:
1. In the literal sense, darkness denotes the absence of visible light: the darkness of night (John 6:17, "it was already dark") or that of dark places. It is the obscurity that our eyes perceive.
2. By extension, the word evokes that which is hidden or concealed: "What I tell you in the dark, speak in the light" (Matthew 10:27) means that what is whispered in secret must be proclaimed publicly.
3. The spiritual and moral sense is dominant: darkness represents ignorance of God, distance from His truth. One who lives without Christ "walks in darkness" (John 8:12), spiritually blinded.
4. More broadly, darkness symbolizes everything that opposes God who is light: sin, death, unbelief. "In Him there is no darkness" says the apostle John of God (1 John 1:5), expressing that the total absence of evil characterizes the Most High.
G4653.origine: The Greek word skotia is close to skotos (darkness) and derives from a root meaning "to cover" or "to obscure." In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words like opel (darkness) and khoshekh (obscurity). This family of words primarily expresses the physical experience of the absence of light, then enriches itself with a theological dimension: darkness becomes the biblical symbol of evil, sin, and separation from God.
G4653.emploi: The word appears about twelve times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels of John and the Johannine epistles, which extensively develop the contrast between light and darkness. John 1:5 sets the fundamental theme: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it." In Matthew and Luke, the word retains a more concrete sense (secret, hidden): what is said in darkness must be proclaimed. In John, the sense dominates: to be in darkness is not to follow Jesus (John 8:12, 12:46), not to know God. The epistle of 1 John deepens this moral and existential opposition: whoever hates his brother "is still in darkness" (1 John 2:9), for living in lies and hatred is incompatible with divine light.
G4653.portee: For the believer, the word darkness invites a clear conscience: to be a Christian is to pass from darkness to light, from ignorance of God to His knowledge. Darkness is not a neutral force, but it symbolizes a state of distance from the Lord that Jesus comes to deliver. This word also reminds us that faith is never merely an intellectual matter: it is a daily walk in the light, away from lies, hatred, and sin. Recognizing darkness is to accept being changed by the luminous presence of Christ.

sens: To deprive of light, to make dark
To cover with darkness, to veil brightness
To confuse, to blur the conscience or judgment
G4654.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to cause to lose light. The sun is obscured when it ceases to shine, as on the days of distress announced in Matthew 24:29 and Mark 13:24: "the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light." It is the darkness that invades the sky.
2. More broadly, it means to cover a surface with darkness or reduce its brightness, as in Revelation 8:12, where "a third of the sun was struck... so that a third of it was darkened." 
3. Figuratively, to obscure refers to the darkening of the mind or moral judgment. In Romans 1:21, hearts without understanding are "plunged into darkness": thoughts are lost, the ability to know God fades. In Romans 11:10, "let their eyes be darkened" means they lose the ability to see spiritually and to understand.
G4654.origine: The word comes from the root σκότος (skótos), which means "darkness" or "obscurity." It is a verb formed from this root to express the action of making dark. In Hebrew, it often corresponds to חָשַׁךְ (hashakh), "to be or become dark." The same Greek word was already used in ancient translations of the Old Testament to translate passages that speak of darkness.
G4654.emploi: This verb appears once in Matthew, once in Mark, once in Luke (in some manuscripts), twice in Romans, and once in Revelation. In the Gospels and Revelation, it describes the cosmic phenomenon of the signs of the end: the stars lose their light, it is an observable event. In Romans, Paul uses it metaphorically to describe what happens to humanity far from God: the human spirit becomes obscured, unable to recognize God, and this obscurity becomes a divine judgment on the refusal of glory given to God. The contrast is strong: the same word designates both a cosmic reality and a spiritual reality.
G4654.portee: This word speaks to us of God's judgment on sin: it blinds the mind and plunges it into ignorance of God. It invites us to examine whether our heart remains open to the light of God or hardens in unbelief. It also reminds us that the end of the world will involve visible and terrifying signs, but that even now, without Christ, the spirit remains obscured — and that in Him, the light shines.

sens: physical absence of light
moral or spiritual opacity, obscurity
domain of Satan and evil
spiritual ignorance, wandering
state of death or separation from God
G4655.detail:
1. Darkness primarily refers to physical obscurity: the darkness that covered the earth during the crucifixion of Jesus (Matthew 27:45) or the darkness of a prison, of a deep night.
2. The word is then used to describe the moral and spiritual state of people distant from God. Ephesians 5:8 states that Christians "were darkness" before their conversion — not only ignorant but enveloped in a reality contrary to that of God.
3. Darkness represents the domain of evil and the father of lies, where ignorance and rebellion against God reign. It is the absolute opposite of divine light.
4. It symbolizes the absence of divine knowledge and spiritual direction: Romans 2:19 speaks of those who "are in darkness" as spiritual blind people.
5. Darkness evokes death, separation, judgment — the absence of God's life-giving presence.
G4655.origine: The Greek word σκότος (skotos) is formed from a root that denotes the lack of light. Its Hebrew equivalent is חֹשֶׁךְ (chosek), very common in the Old Testament. In ancient Greek, this word initially applied to natural darkness, but the authors of the New Testament imbued it with profound spiritual meanings: according to ancient biblical symbolism, darkness becomes the preferred image of evil, lies, and ignorance opposed to God.
G4655.emploi: The word appears 30 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul’s letters and in John. It is used in four main contexts: first, physical darkness (Matthew 27:45, Luke 23:44), signs of judgment or death; then, the spiritual state of non-believers, often in contrast with light (Ephesians 5:8, 1 Thessalonians 5:5); next, the organized domain of evil and Satan (Ephesians 6:12, Colossians 1:13); finally, ignorance of God and the need for conversion (Acts 26:18). The word takes on an increasingly broad scope, from the visible to the invisible, from the tangible to the moral.
G4655.portee: Understanding darkness in the Bible means grasping that sin is not merely a weakness: it is confinement, blindness, a domain of slavery. But the Bible uses this word to remind us that Jesus came "to shine the light" (2 Corinthians 4:6) and that in Him, we have passed from darkness to light. This image invites us to view our Christian life not as a series of isolated acts, but as a passage from one kingdom to another.

sens: To make dark, deprive of light
To cover with darkness, with shadows
To confuse, disturb understanding
G4656.detail:
1. To darken primarily means to make physically dark, to deprive of light. This is what happens in Revelation 9:2, where the smoke rising from the abyss darkens the sun and the air: clarity disappears under a layer of darkness.
2. The word also describes the action of completely covering a region with darkness. In Revelation 16:10, the kingdom of the beast is covered with thick darkness, so intense that the inhabitants suffer physically.
3. Figuratively, to darken means to trouble or veil the mind, the understanding. In Ephesians 4:18, the Apostle Paul states that the understanding of the Gentiles is darkened — they no longer see clearly, they no longer comprehend the truth of God due to ignorance and the hardening of the heart.
G4656.origine: The verb σκοτόω comes from the noun σκότος (skótos), "the darkness" or "the shadows." It translates into Greek several Hebrew roots such as חָשַׁךְ ("to be dark"), whose basic image is the absence of light. In Hebrew, darkness is often associated with judgment, sin, or distance from God. The Greek verb adds the idea of an action: something or someone makes things obscure.
G4656.emploi: The verb σκοτόω appears three times in the New Testament. In Revelation 9:2, it describes an impressive natural phenomenon: the smoke from the abyss darkens the sky. In Revelation 16:10, it characterizes one of the eschatological judgments, where darkness becomes a punishment. In Ephesians 4:18, Paul uses it in the passive and figurative sense to express that the spirit of non-believers is veiled — unable to perceive the light of God. This is the only truly spiritual and metaphorical use of the term in the New Testament.
G4656.portee: This word reminds us that spiritual ignorance is real and that it darkens understanding. It is not merely an absence of knowledge, but an active covering that prevents seeing the truth. For believers, the challenge is to ask God to keep us from such darkness of heart and mind, and to allow us to walk in His light.

sens: Trash, waste, repugnant matter
By extension: anything despicable, worthless
G4657.detail:
1. The word literally refers to trash, refuse, excrement — everything that is thrown away because it is vile and unusable. It is the worst of deposits, what is trampled underfoot without scruple.
2. Paul uses it figuratively in Philippians 3:8 to express his absolute disdain for everything that could have made him proud in the past (his status, his religious accomplishments): he considers them as dung, vile and repugnant things, because the knowledge of Christ surpasses everything else infinitely. It is the strongest image to say "I count this as nothing."
G4657.origine: The Greek word skúbalon properly denotes trash, fecal matter, anything that is rejected. Its exact etymology is debated, but the meaning is stable: it is what is abandoned, what is refused. The Greek version of the Old Testament uses it in Ben Sirach to describe what accumulates at the bottom of a sieve. It is a crude, straightforward word: it paints the lowest reality to oppose it to the supreme worth of Christ.
G4657.emploi: Paul uses this word only once, in Philippians 3:8, at the heart of his spiritual autobiography. He draws a striking contrast: once he would have counted his religious and social advantages as gains (being an Israelite, a Pharisee, a zealot for the law), but now he judges them as dung, filth to be rejected. This total reversal of value expresses the radical break that the encounter with Christ caused in the apostle. The word, rare and violent, emphasizes the intensity of the change.
G4657.portee: For the reader, this word liberates: it says that everything we once relied on — our status, our achievements, our reputation — can suddenly become nothing if we find in Christ what truly has value. This is not a sad renunciation moral, but an explosion of joy before a discovered wealth. It invites everyone to ask: what do I hold as "gain" in my life, and does the excellence of knowing Christ truly surpass everything else?

sens: Inhabitant of Scythia, an ancient region of Asia (southern Russia and present-day Siberia)
In the eyes of the Greeks, a representative of the wildest and most barbaric people
G4658.detail:
1. The Scythians are the inhabitants of Scythia, a region located north of the Mediterranean kingdoms, in the steppes of what is now Russia and Siberia. They are a nomadic people far removed from the centers of Greco-Roman civilization.
2. For the Greeks and Romans, the name "Scythian" became synonymous with extreme barbarism and savagery. In Colossians 3:11, Paul uses it to symbolize the height of cultural strangeness and distance from civilization, alongside the term "barbarian": these Scythians embody, in the eyes of Mediterranean readers, the most raw and uncivilized humanity.
G4658.origine: The Greek term Σκύθης refers to the inhabitant of Σκυθία (Scythia), the land of the Scythians. They are a real people, well-known to ancient Greek and Roman authors. The Scythians' reputation for savagery stemmed from their nomadic lifestyle, warrior customs, and geographical distance from Greco-Roman urban centers, which made them almost legendary and threatening in the eyes of the civilized Mediterranean.
G4658.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 3:11. Paul lists all the human barriers that the Gospel transcends: Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian or Scythian, slave or free. By placing "Scythian" immediately after "barbarian," Paul emphasizes his point: even the people considered the most uncivilized and exotic are not excluded from Christ's call and unity. This unique mention underscores the radical universality of the Gospel.
G4658.portee: By mentioning the Scythians, Paul reminds the readers in Colossae that the Gospel knows no geographical boundaries or hierarchy of civilization. One who comes from the most despised or distant culture has as much access to grace and unity in Christ as a respectable Roman citizen. It is a powerful invitation to welcome the Other, even those who seem the most strange or distant to us.

sens: Having a dark, closed, or downcast face
Expressing melancholy or sorrow through one's expression
Intentionally displaying sadness to impress others
G4659.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a facial expression: someone who is "sad" has a furrowed brow, contracted features, like someone dark or morose. It is the outward appearance that speaks first, well before words.
2. This expression reflects an inner state: melancholy, sorrow, or simply a dark mood. To the disciples gathered after the crucifixion, Jesus asks: "What are you discussing as you walk along? Why are you so sad?" (Luke 24:17) — he sees their downcast faces and knows they are troubled.
3. The word can also refer to a displayed sadness, a facade: Jesus warns hypocrites who fast "with a sad face" (Matthew 6:16), meaning they make their faces look disfigured so that others see them suffer. It is a theatrical sadness, for show.
G4659.origine: The word is composed of two Greek roots: "skuthrós" (dark, morose) and "ôps" (the look, the aspect of the face). The image is that of a dark face, closed off from the light. It is a word that primarily concerns the body, the visible expression, rather than the hidden soul.
G4659.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Matthew 6:16, Jesus denounces hypocrites who affect a look of suffering so that others admire their piety. In Luke 24:17, it appears instead to sincerely describe the state of the disciples: their sad faces reveal their distress after Jesus' death. In both cases, the word concerns what is visible: the face, the demeanor, the countenance. The Bible borrows it from the Greek Old Testament (Genesis 40:7) to refer to servants who look unwell.
G4659.portee: This word reminds us that the face does not lie: it betrays the state of the heart. It invites the reader to examine their own face when they pray or fast — not to suffer in public, but to ensure that their actions are not a performance. It is a call to authenticity: true devotion does not seek to be seen; it arises from the sincerity of the heart.

sens: To skin, to tear (ancient meaning)
To torment someone, to harass
To disturb someone by incessantly soliciting them
To cause distress or fatigue
To wear down or exhaust morally
G4660.detail:
1. In ancient Greek, the word originally meant to skin or tear the skin. This is the primitive image of the verb, but it has disappeared from the texts of the New Testament.
2. The meaning has expanded to include tormenting someone morally, harassing or troubling them. When the centurion in Luke 7:6 says, "Do not trouble yourself," he fears troubling Jesus by forcing him to come.
3. To trouble means to disturb someone repeatedly or inopportunely, to solicit them incessantly against their will. The friends of the synagogue leader say to Jesus: "Why trouble the teacher any further?" (Mark 5:35), meaning why continue to disturb him with your requests?
4. The word also expresses the state of one who is touched, shaken internally, like the weary crowd in Matthew 9:36, tired and downcast, demoralized like sheep without a shepherd.
5. In the biblical context, languishing or being troubled describes a deep moral and spiritual fatigue.
G4660.origine: The root evokes the idea of tearing or ripping. In classical Greek, the verb had this brutal physical meaning. Over time, the meaning softened and became figurative: it shifts from "to skin" to "to torment the soul," then to "to trouble," "to fatigue." This is a natural process where the concrete image becomes moral. The word belongs to a Greek family expressing violence, but in Christian texts, it describes more an internal suffering or an unwelcome solicitation.
G4660.emploi: The verb σκύλλω appears four times in the Gospel: in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Mark 5:35 and Luke 8:49 report the same event (the death of the synagogue leader's daughter): people ask why to trouble Jesus any further since all is lost. Luke 7:6 shows the centurion refusing to trouble Jesus by asking him to enter his house: this is an act of respect and humility. Matthew 9:36 uses the passive participle "weary" to describe the crowd: they are troubled, morally exhausted, without a guide. Thus, the word shifts from the meaning of "to disturb" (with a subject that troubles) to the meaning of "to be in moral distress" (with a subject that suffers).
G4660.portee: This verb speaks of the respect we must show to those who help us, as the centurion demonstrates before Jesus. It invites us not to abuse the availability of others with repeated and indiscreet requests. But it also describes the state of the crowd: a weary, demoralized humanity, languishing without a true guide. It is an image of the human heart before encountering the shepherd who restores it.

sens: The weapons and goods taken from a defeated enemy
What is forcibly taken from someone
The loot, the fruit of victory
G4661.detail:
1. A spoil is primarily the collection of weapons that are seized from an enemy after defeating them in battle. It is the material trophy of victory: the armor, the swords, everything that constituted the strength of the vanquished. In Luke 11:22, Jesus speaks of one who "distributes his spoils" — the weapons of the strong man he has subdued.
2. In a broader sense, a spoil refers to anything that can be stolen or seized from someone: their goods, their possessions. It is what is taken when one plunders or wins a victory.
3. Figuratively, it symbolizes triumph: the one who possesses the spoils has achieved a complete and undeniable victory.
G4661.origine: The Greek word σκῦλον comes from a root meaning "to strip away," "to take away." In Hebrew, it is often the word שָׁלָל (chaal) that is found to express this idea of loot and spoils taken from an enemy. The word always evokes the idea of violent appropriation and material victory.
G4661.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 11:22, in a parable where Jesus compares two strong men. The stronger one defeats the other and "takes away all the weapons in which he trusted, and distributes his spoils." Jesus uses this image of spoils to show that the more powerful one takes back everything that the first possessed. It is an image of total domination and definitive victory.
G4661.portee: This parable of the spoils invites the believer to recognize who is truly the strongest: the one who can really take away our weapons and defenses. It raises the question of who will dominate us and who will have the final word. For the one who believes in Christ, this image reminds us that He alone possesses true power and can free us from what binds us.

sens: Devoured by worms that eat away at the flesh
Stricken by a putrid and degrading disease
G4662.detail:
1. The word literally describes a body eaten away, decomposed by worms — an image of physical disintegration and decay. In Acts 12:23, King Herod Agrippa, who allowed himself to be acclaimed as a god, suddenly dies from a disease where worms eat him alive: this is the mark of divine judgment on his pride.
2. In a broader figurative sense, it is the image of total corruption and degradation inflicted by God — not only a physical death, but a shameful death, showing that one who rises against God will be brought low to their destruction.
G4662.origine: The Greek word is composed of two roots: "sképhis" (worm) and "bibróskô" (to eat, to gnaw). It is a poetic and vivid formation to describe what is eaten by worms. The image of worms devouring flesh also appears in other ancient Jewish texts to denote divine punishment (see 2 Maccabees 9:9, which recounts the death of King Antiochus with the same motif).
G4662.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 12:23, to describe the death of King Herod Agrippa. It is used dramatically: at the very moment Herod accepts the acclamations of the people who deify him, an angel of the Lord strikes him, and he dies eaten by worms. It is a visible and immediate act of judgment, reminding the reader that God alone deserves glory and punishes those who claim it for themselves.
G4662.portee: This account teaches that the claim to glory and the refusal to acknowledge God lead to total ruin — not only to death, but to a degrading death. For the Christian reader, it serves as a reminder that all honor and authority come from God, and that appropriating His glory is the worst of sins. It is also a warning against pride and a call to give to God alone the glory that belongs to Him.

sens: Invertebrate animal that feeds on corpses
Creature symbolizing the degradation and decay of the dead body
Instrument of divine punishment in the afterlife
G4663.detail:
