Finally, it invites every believer to cultivate a similar compassion, which flows from their very innards and does not remain locked away.

sens: Porous and absorbent object used for cleaning or soaking up a liquid
Instrument used at the crucifixion of Jesus to give him vinegar to drink
G4699.detail:
1. A sponge is a porous and spongy object capable of absorbing and retaining liquids. It is a cleaning utensil or for applying liquids, very useful for soaking, imbibing, and cleaning. In the three Gospel passages (Matthew 27:48, Mark 15:36, John 19:29), a sponge soaked in vinegar is used to quench Jesus' thirst on the cross.
2. The sponge becomes the concrete symbol of the last drink offered to the dying Jesus: a gesture that is both mocking (the vinegar being the ordinary drink of soldiers, cheap and bitter) and of silent pity. The fact that all four Gospels report this detail — with variations (attached to a reed in Matthew and Mark, to a branch of hyssop in John) — shows its importance in the passion narrative.
G4699.origine: The Greek word σπόγγος (spongos) literally designates a porous object that absorbs moisture. It is likely of Eastern origin, like most names of materials and objects in Mediterranean trade. The word is common in the Greek of the time, both in biblical texts and in secular literature. The sponge was well known to ancient peoples as a practical utensil.
G4699.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, and always in the account of the crucifixion. Matthew 27:48 and Mark 15:36 describe the scene almost identically: someone fills a sponge with vinegar, attaches it to a reed, and gives it to Jesus to drink. John 19:29 reports an additional detail: the sponge is attached to a branch of hyssop (a small plant), which raises a question of physical consistency — hyssop being fragile to hold weight — but perhaps emphasizes a liturgical symbolism (hyssop being used in the purifications of the Law). The sponge soaked in vinegar is the last gesture towards Jesus before his death.
G4699.portee: The sponge and vinegar symbolize the extreme humiliation of Jesus as death approaches: an ordinary, cheap, bitter drink offered in a rudimentary manner. This detail reminds us that the passion is nothing heroic or glorious in the eyes of the world; it is a death amid mockery and indifference. At the same time, the fact that all the Gospels report this gesture shows that nothing escapes God's attention — even the ultimate sufferings of His Son.

sens: Armed man who attacks and robs on the roads or in cities
Member of the Sicarii, a group of Jewish revolutionaries from the 1st century who committed political assassinations
G4607.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a violent man who hides to rob travelers or terrorize cities — a dangerous criminal armed with a short sword that he conceals under his clothing. This is the most concrete meaning: a highwayman.
2. In Judea in the 1st century, the Sicarii formed a group of Jewish revolutionaries who waged armed struggle against Roman occupation by committing political murders. When the Roman commander asks Paul, "Are you not that Egyptian who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand assassins out into the wilderness?" (Acts 21:38), he is referring to these dangerous and organized insurgents.
G4607.origine: The word comes from the Latin "sica," which refers to a short sword or dagger. The Sicarii derived their name from this weapon they carried concealed. This is how Roman and Jewish historians of the time referred to them — not as mere thieves, but as an armed political faction.
G4607.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 21:38. The Roman commander mentions an Egyptian who had revolted and gathered four thousand brigands in the wilderness. This episode reflects the real political tensions of 1st century Judea: the Sicarii were a known threat, feared by the Roman authorities and mentioned in the chronicles of the time. Paul is suspected of being one — evidence that this group terrorized the region.
G4607.portee: This term reminds the reader that the politics of 1st century Judea were violent, marked by uprisings against Rome. It sheds light on the context of hostility and danger in which Paul carries out his ministry: he is confronted with a society agitated by divisions and conflicting messianic expectations.

sens: fermented alcoholic beverage, stronger than ordinary wine
that which disturbs the mind and removes clarity
symbol of that which distracts from the service of God
G4608.detail:
1. It is an alcoholic beverage produced by fermentation, like wine, but generally stronger and often made from fruits or grains other than grapes — honey, dates, barley, for example. In Luke 1:15, the angel Gabriel forbids Zacharias from giving this drink to his son John, as well as ordinary wine.
2. The word evokes drunkenness and loss of reason: it "intoxicates" the one who drinks it. This is why the Law of Moses prohibited it for priests serving in the temple (see the Hebrew root שׁכר, which means "to be drunk").
3. Spiritually, it symbolizes that which diverts a believer from his mission. John the Baptist, called to prepare the way of the Lord, was to remain completely in control of his mind — which is why he would abstain from it even from his mother's womb.
G4608.origine: The word comes from Aramaic שִׁכְרָא (shikrâ), borrowed from Greek σίκερα. It translates the Hebrew שֵׁכָר (shékhar), whose root means "to be drunk" or "to intoxicate." In the Greek Old Testament, this term refers to any fermented drink capable of disturbing the mind, contrasting with wine (οἶνος), which was the common beverage. It is a Semitic word that became Hellenistic.
G4608.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:15, in the declaration of the angel Gabriel to Zacharias regarding the birth of John the Baptist. This prohibition is in line with the Old Testament, where the Law prohibited any alcoholic beverage for the serving priest (see Leviticus 10:9). The absence of this drink symbolizes the total consecration and sobriety of mind required to fulfill the mission that God entrusts to John — to announce the coming of the Messiah.
G4608.portee: This word reminds Christians that sobriety of body and mind is a sign of consecration. It is not an end in itself, but a means to remain available to the Holy Spirit and to the will of God. The example of John the Baptist invites us to examine what may diminish our spiritual clarity and our ability to hear God.
